hpi_details: 32M presents with severe pain, blistering, and peeling skin on the back of both hands after boiling water spilled on them 2 hours ago. Skin is red, wet, and extremely tender to touch.
ideas: thinks he has severe burns and needs dressings
concerns: worried about permanent scarring and hand function

clinical_knowledge.topic: Thermal Burn Injury evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Thermal Burn Injury is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Partial-Thickness (Second-Degree) Thermal Burn of bilateral hands, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: painful redness, blisters, and peeling skin on both hands after boiling water spill

Key HPI features: 32M presents with severe pain, blistering, and peeling skin on the back of both hands after boiling water spilled on them 2 hours ago. Skin is red, wet, and extremely tender to touch.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Partial-Thickness (Second-Degree) Thermal Burn of bilateral hands.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Thermal Burn Injury.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Chemical burn without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Inhalation injury (soot in mouth, hoarseness).
management_principles: Assess burn depth, total body surface area, neurovascular status, tetanus status, and hand function; burns involving the hands merit burn-specialist consultation.

After cooling and cleansing, dressings, analgesia, and any blister management should be selected by a clinician based on depth, contamination, allergies, and local protocol; avoid routine silver sulfadiazine for superficial partial-thickness burns when a better healing dressing is available.
Begin guided range-of-motion therapy when appropriate and give clear return precautions for infection, worsening pain, numbness, or impaired circulation.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

Skin is red, wet, and extremely tender to touch.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Partial-Thickness (Second-Degree) Thermal Burn of bilateral hands.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Partial-Thickness (Second-Degree) Thermal Burn of bilateral hands.
reference_soap.plan: Cool the injury with running water if still within a useful early window; do not apply ice. Assess depth, total body surface area, tetanus status, circulation, and hand function, and obtain burn-specialist input because both hands are involved. Use clinician-selected nonadherent dressings and analgesia, with guided early motion when safe; urgently escalate numbness, pale or cool digits, severe swelling, infection, or breathing symptoms.

teaching.one_liner: Tissue injury caused by heat exposure, requiring assessment of total body surface area (TBSA), depth, and airway involvement.

must_ask.say: What caused the burn: an open flame, hot liquid, steam, or chemicals?
Were you trapped in an enclosed space, and do you have hoarseness or black soot in your cough?
Which body parts were burned: face, chest, arms, or legs?
Are the burned areas extremely painful and blistered, or numb and white?
Did you cool the burn with clean running water, and what first aid or pain medicine have you used?

history.answer: I spilled boiling water over both of my hands at work two hours ago, and now the skin is bright red, blistered, and burning terribly.
A large pot of boiling water slipped while I was moving it on the kitchen stove, splashing directly across the backs of both hands.
It happened about two hours ago, around noon right in the middle of our restaurant lunch rush.
The burn is on the backs of both hands and across my knuckles, covering an area about the size of each palm.
It was plain boiling water from cooking pasta, and it splashed on me for just a split second before I pulled away.
I ran cool tap water over both hands for about ten minutes right after it happened, but I didn't put ice or any creams on them.
No, it was just hot water in an open kitchen, not an enclosed room fire, and there was no flame or smoke.
No hoarseness, my voice feels normal, and I don't have any shortness of breath or cough.
The pain is an excruciating 8 out of 10 throbbing ache, and every part of the burn is super sensitive—there are no numb spots.
My fingers feel tight and swollen when I try to bend them, but I can still move them and feel my fingertips normally.
No, my palms, the undersides of my fingers, and my wrists were completely spared; the burns don't go all the way around.
There was no deep gash or heavy spurting blood, just clear liquid weeping from where the blisters popped.
No, it was clean boiling tap water from a clean stainless steel cooking pot, with no dirt, rust, or foreign objects.
No, it wasn't an animal or human bite.
The redness appeared immediately from the heat, but there isn't any foul-smelling yellow pus or red streaks traveling up my arms.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, dizziness, or lightheadedness.
No, my skin was completely healthy and normal until the spill two hours ago.
No, I am on my feet all day working in the kitchen and have never been bedridden or had pressure sores.
It was an accidental spill while lifting a heavy pot; nobody assaulted me, and I did not harm myself.
I received a tetanus booster shot about five or six years ago after a minor knife cut at work.
I think these are severe second-degree burns and I need medical dressings before they get infected.
I work as a professional chef, so I'm terrified this might cause permanent scarring or ruin my hand mobility and livelihood.
I'm hoping you can give me something strong for this pain, apply proper sterile dressings, and tell me how to heal without scars.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or kidney disease.
I have never had any surgeries and I've never been hospitalized for anything.
I do not take any prescription medications, steroids, or blood thinners.
I don't have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I drink a beer or two on the weekend with friends, but I don't drink heavily.
I work full-time as a restaurant chef and live in an apartment with my partner.
Both of my parents are alive and healthy, and there is no family history of circulatory or skin disorders.

exam.finding: The patient appears alert and oriented, in visible distress from bilateral hand pain, holding both hands elevated and protected.
Blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Nasal vibrissae are intact, and the oral cavity and posterior pharynx show no soot, mucosal erythema, blister formation, or edema.
Auscultation reveals clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, stridor, rhonchi, or crackles.
Heart sounds are regular without murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.

Both dorsal hands demonstrate bright red, wet weeping surfaces with thin-walled bullae, deroofed skin, brisk blanching, and extreme tenderness, sparing the palms and spanning approximately 2% total body surface area.
Radial and ulnar pulses are 2+ bilaterally, and digital capillary refill is brisk at under two seconds in all ten digits.
Two-point discrimination and light touch sensation are intact across all palmar digital surfaces bilaterally, while dorsal burned skin displays marked hyperesthesia.
Active and passive flexion and extension of all digits and wrists are preserved, although full fist formation is limited by dorsal pain and swelling, with no extensor tendon exposure.
